title: Blindspots Week 1 Wisdom
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: The talk explores the concept of wisdom in Buddhism, which involves recognizing the causal relationship between actions and their consequences, rather than judging things as good or bad. This means observing how certain behaviors lead to suffering and understanding the impermanence of all things. Wisdom is not about imposing a fixed standard, but rather about cultivating discernment through inquiry and attention, allowing us to see patterns and connections that may have been previously overlooked. By developing wisdom, we can gain clarity and insight into our lives, cutting through deception and ego, and ultimately experiencing a deeper understanding of reality.

sentences.text: So in studying how a new exposure to the teachings of the women ancestors can impact us, let's at the same time continue to work with the rest of the package of Buddhism.
For example, during the Wednesday evening dharma talks we've been studying the seven factors of awakening, and we've just started to touch into the seventh factor of awakening, which is wisdom.
So here are some thoughts on wisdom, and we'll see where that goes in future months.
Might present wisdom as being the discernment of what is skillful or spiritually wholesome.
For example, observing that acting out of habit leads to suffering and recognizing the causal relationship between habit and suffering is wisdom.
Wisdom is a recognition of karma.
Karma is just about causation.
Say the consequences of feeding certain of our desires lead to suffering: there's a causal connection.
A common error made with karma is trying to search for causes beyond our experience.
Why did this illness happen to her?
Similar to when we try to apply the precepts to other people.
Precepts we undertake as a tool for our own growth.
So one danger in karma is trying to apply it to other people, and another danger is that the factors of causation are largely unknown and complex, and we can notice patterns in them.
So one of the days this week I put my hat on the roof of my car and drove to work, and when I got to work it wasn't still there.
So I emailed Diane, because this was actually Monday night, so I was doing the class and knew I wasn't going to get home.
I emailed Diane and said, I'm not going to be home until late, you're coming home during the light, would you keep an eye out for it by the road.
And she went and she emailed a few people in her neighborhood who she knows walk every day.
And one of our neighbors who is out walking saw this hat hanging from a tree branch.
It looks good there, it must belong there.
And he got home and his wife said, hey, you got an email.
Dallas lost his hat, you didn't happen to see it, did you?
And he's like, oh yeah, it's hanging from a tree branch.
He went and got it.
And then he emailed me and said he had it, and I thought, wow, that's interesting, the hat must have got caught as the car was driving by.
And then another neighbor said to her husband when he came home, hey, Dallas lost his hat, you didn't happen to see it, did you?
And he said, well yeah.
And by this time when they talked it was ten o'clock at night.
He said, yeah, I saw it and I hung it from a tree branch.
And she said, oh, we've got to go get it.
So she ran out and ran to the car and realized that she had locked a stray tomcat in her car, and let the tomcat go.
And her car is probably a lot better off for that cat having been let out and not being in there all night.
I've just been thinking about that today.
That's a good example: you don't know the causes and complexities of karma, right?
Moving on, distinguishing between judgment and discernment might be confusing.
Judgment is our human tendency to classify everything that arises as good or bad.
Discernment is a recognition of the causal relationship, for example between certain behaviors and suffering.
Wisdom or discernment doesn't say that anything is good or bad.
It just says if you do this more, that seems to happen more.
If your intention is more of this, then you might do more of that.

If you observe that daily meditation leads to more seeing, more attentiveness to other people, then maybe you undertake daily meditation, with the result that there is more attentiveness to other people.
Kind of like our walking on State Street to the co-op.
We didn't walk on State Street because we judged that State Street is good and Maple Street is bad.
We discern that the route to the co-op is State Street.
It's really interesting because my co-op is on Forest Street.
So wisdom recognizes the impermanence of all things.
I'm going to go to somebody else's words now.
Shambhala teacher Judy Leaf cautions against static, closed-minded wisdom.
She finds its roots in the inquisitiveness and fundamental questioning that bubbles forth when we pay attention to our attention.
Through this pointed questioning that punctures delusions, we penetrate to the emptiness of all the risings.
In the article "The Sharp Sword of Prajna" she reviews some wonderfully useful symbols of wisdom or prajna.
She writes:
*The sharpness of prajna cuts at many levels.
In the mundane sense prajna represents a sharpening of perception and inquisitiveness.
As we go about our lives and particularly as we enter a spiritual path we are always raising questions.
We are always trying to understand.
Instead of just accepting a superficial understanding we think deeply and ask what do I really understand?
Does any of this make any sense whatsoever?
Prajna has this quality of creative doubt.
Not just accepting things based on authority or hearsay but continually digging deeper.
The sword of prajna has two sharp sides not just one.
It is a double bladed sword sharp on both sides so when you make a stroke of prajna or wisdom it cuts two ways.
When you cut through deception you are also cutting through egos taking credit for that.
You are left nowhere more or less.*
Another image for prajna is the sun.
The sun of prajna is illuminating our world.
If we are inquisitive, if we are attentive, a kind of natural illumination happens.
There is light shining on the dark corners and a sense of being under the spotlight, totally exposed.
A lot of times we take the approach of not really wanting to look too closely at ourselves or at our lives.
We just look the other way and move on.
However, there is no corner where the sun of prajna isn't shining.
Prajna is like having a sun shining all around everywhere, never setting.
Prajna is also represented iconographically by the feminine deity prajnaparamita and the masculine deity manjushri.
Prajnaparamita is depicted as a beautiful feminine deity with four arms.
Two arms are folded on her lap in the classic posture of meditation, and her two other arms hold a sword and a book.
Through these gestures she manifests three aspects of prajna: academic knowledge, cutting through deception, and direct perception of emptiness.
So we will come back to those three.
We've got an exercise together coming up, and then we'll take a koan home, and maybe we can sit with that koan with academic knowledge, cutting through deception and direct perception of emptiness.
